name: Telugu
variety: Modern Standard Telugu (educated speech of coastal Andhra Pradesh), formal style
sources: Bhaskararao, Peri and Ray, Arpita (2017). Telugu. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 47(2) (Illustrations of the IPA).
Krishnamurti, Bh. and Gwynn, J. P. L. (1985). A Grammar of Modern Telugu. Delhi: Oxford University Press.
Krishnamurti, Bh. (1998). Telugu. In Steever (ed.), The Dravidian Languages. London: Routledge.
Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju (2003). The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Kostić, Djordje; Mitter, Alokananda; Krishnamurti, Bh. (1977). A Short Outline of Telugu Phonetics. Calcutta: Indian Statistical Institute.
Abercrombie, David (1967). Elements of General Phonetics. Edinburgh University Press.
Murty, Lalita; Otake, Takashi; Cutler, Anne (2007). Perceptual tests of rhythmic similarity: I. Mora rhythm. Language and Speech 50(1).
contrasts: vowel length for five vowel qualities
single versus geminate consonants, for nearly every consonant

voiced versus voiceless stops in all vocabulary; aspirated and breathy voiced stops in the learned (Sanskrit) and loan vocabulary, giving a four-way laryngeal contrast in educated speech that colloquial speech reduces to two
dental versus retroflex stops; alveolar versus retroflex nasal and lateral
/æː/ is marginal: it contrasts with /aː/ and /eː/ in past-tense verb forms and in English loans and has no letter of its own
three sibilants /s ʂ ɕ/ in educated speech, merged to /s/ by many speakers
allophony: /tʃ dʒ/ are alveolar affricates [ts dz] before the non-front vowels /a aː u uː o oː/ and palato-alveolar [tʃ dʒ] before front vowels in native words; [tʃ dʒ] before back vowels occur in Sanskrit and other loans, so the two pairs are marginally contrastive; urban speech increasingly uses [tʃ dʒ] everywhere
the written nasal (anusvara) is homorganic with a following stop: [ŋ] before velars, [ɲ] before palatals, [ɳ] before retroflexes, [n̪] before dentals, [m] before labials; word-finally it is [m]
/n/ is dental before dental stops and alveolar elsewhere
/r/ is a tap [ɾ] between vowels and a short trill when geminate or in careful speech
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant, closer to [w] before rounded vowels
word-initial /e eː/ take a [j] on-glide and /o oː/ a [w] on-glide
/e eː o oː/ are reported to be more open when the next syllable has a low vowel
aspirated and breathy voiced stops lose their aspiration in colloquial speech
word-final short vowels are very short and are elided before a vowel-initial word (sandhi)
phonotactics: native words end in a vowel; consonant-final words are loans or end in the nasal written with anusvara ([m])
initial clusters are mostly consonant plus /r/ or occur in Sanskrit and English loans
medial clusters are chiefly geminates and homorganic nasal plus stop
retroflex /ɳ ɭ/ do not occur word-initially
vowel harmony in short high vowels: a medial or suffix vowel alternates between [i] and [u] in agreement with the following vowel (gadi 'room', gadulu 'rooms'; dative -ki after i, -ku elsewhere)

stress.type: no lexical stress; weak, not contrastive
stress.rule: Word prominence is slight and descriptions disagree on its place: usually the first syllable, with a heavy syllable (long vowel or closed syllable) near the start of the word able to attract it.
stress.cues: phrase-level pitch movement and the greater duration of heavy syllables; no reduction of vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none; short vowels in non-initial open syllables are shortened and final vowels may be elided in connected speech, without change of category
rhythm.notes: Abercrombie (1967) named Telugu as a syllable-timed language. Later perceptual work groups it with Japanese as mora-based (Murty, Otake and Cutler 2007): syllable duration depends on vowel length and on coda or geminate consonants. No published nPVI value is cited here.

length.notes: Long vowels are roughly twice as long as short vowels and geminate closures roughly twice as long as single ones (approximate ratios from acoustic descriptions; no exact figures cited).

intonation.declarative: non-final phrases start low and rise toward their end; the final phrase, normally the verb, falls to low
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clitic -ā on the questioned word or on the verb, with statement word order; pitch rises on the lengthened clitic vowel
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main peak, followed by a fall to low
intonation.continuation: rise to a high boundary at the end of non-final phrases and non-finite clauses
intonation.accent_shape: low at the start of the phrase with a rise to its right edge (LH); no pitch accents tied to lexical stress
intonation.notes: Instrumental work on Telugu intonation is sparse; this follows the reference grammars and the general pattern described for the neighbouring Dravidian languages.

phonation: breathy voiced (voiced aspirated) stops /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/ in learned vocabulary

problems: anusvara ం is always [n]: word-final -ం comes out as [n] instead of [m] (పుస్తకం gives [pustakan]) and it does not assimilate to the next stop (సంపద [sanpada], అంగడి [anɡaɖi])
చ and జ are always palatal [c ɟ]; the alveolar affricates [ts dz] before back vowels are produced only for the rarely written letters ౘ and ౙ
no /æː/; it cannot be read off the spelling and te_list has no entries for it
in the phoneme table short a carries the lng flag while the long vowels do not; the table is headed 'these are only guesses' and the voice is marked 'status testing'
stress is fixed on the first syllable with stress-accent settings
ర and ఱ are always the trill R2; no tap between vowels
only word-initial short ఎ gets a [j] on-glide; initial ఏ, ఒ and ఓ get no on-glide
good: vowel length (short 110 to 130, long 270 to 300 in table units) and geminates (doubled consonant phonemes) are kept
dental, retroflex, aspirated and breathy voiced stops come from the Hindi base table
వ is the approximant [ʋ], not a fricative

notes: Most Telugu words end in a vowel. The spelling shows vowel length and gemination directly, so both can be read from the text; [ts dz] and /æː/ cannot.
